title: The analyses of precipitation processes in the microstructure of S31035 steel after ageing at 750 °C
abstract: Abstract This paper presents the results of the analysis of the precipitation process in S31035 (22Cr25Ni3W3CuCoNbN) steel after long-term ageing at 750 °C for up to 30,000 h. The identification of precipitates was carried out using selective electron diffraction with FEI TITAN 80–300 transmission electron microscope. In the microstructure of the test steel in the as-received condition, the primary precipitates of Z phase were revealed. Ageing has contributed to the precipitation of secondary phases at the grain boundaries, twin boundaries and inside the grains. At the grain boundaries, M 23 C 6  carbides and Laves phase precipitates were revealed during the initial period of ageing. Longer ageing times resulted in the occurrence of sigma phase and G phase particles at the boundaries. Only M 23 C 6  carbides were observed at the twin boundaries. In turn, inside the grains, the presence of ε_Cu particles, Laves phase and secondary Z phase precipitates was demonstrated. In addition, single complexes of precipitates consisting of the primary Z phase particles and M 23 C 6  carbides nucleating on them as well as the Laves phase precipitates were revealed near the grain boundaries.
journal: Archives of Civil and Mechanical Engineering

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Despite the growing share of renewable energy sources (RES) in electricity production, mandated by the European Union (EU) climate policy, conventional fossil-fuel combustion units and nuclear power plants remain the primary, stable sources of energy generation. However, RES are unstable and intermittent energy sources, dependent on weather conditions and the geographic location of a given region [ 1 ]. Coal-fired power units are reliable energy sources that provide continuous, independent power unaffected by the factors mentioned above. A reduction in the negative environmental impact of conventional power units primarily involves improving their performance parameters [ 2 ] to achieve at least 50% efficiency. The improvement of steam parameters was enabled, among other things, by the development and implementation of modern creep- and heat-resistant construction materials, such as bainitic, martensitic, and austenitic steels, as well as nickel-based alloys [ 3 ].

The group of modern austenitic steels for use at (ultra)supercritical parameters includes S31035 steel. This steel was developed at the end of the 1990s in Sweden under the European Thermal AD 700 program, which aimed to prepare a new type of power unit with an efficiency of approximately 50%. That program also involved the development of new construction materials with a stable microstructure, high mechanical properties and the required corrosion and steam oxidation resistance during service at 700 °C [ 4 ]. The microstructural stability of austenitic steels, as demonstrated by previous studies, is primarily due to precipitation processes at the grain/twin boundaries and within the grains. In creep-resistant austenitic steels, different precipitation sequences may occur in their microstructures [ 5 ], depending on their chemical composition and temperature-time parameters. The stability, volume fraction, morphology and precipitation sequence are decisive factors affecting not only the creep resistance, but also the corrosion resistance of these materials [ 6 ].

Prior studies on S31035 steel have focused on evaluating its corrosion resistance [ 7 ], low-cycle fatigue resistance [ 8 ] and microstructural changes following fatigue [ 9 ], as well as analysing the microstructure [ 10 ] and degradation processes [ 11 ]. Precipitation processes are the primary mechanism of degradation for the microstructure and mechanical properties [ 12 ] of austenitic heat-resistant steels. For S31035 steel, these processes have been reported so far only after short ageing times up to 1000 h [ 13 ]. In contrast to other heat-resistant alloys with an austenitic matrix, the available literature lacks comprehensive data on precipitation of secondary phase particles during long-term ageing. Microscopic examination of heat-resistant alloys after extended ageing at temperatures close to those expected during service provides a more accurate understanding of their degradation mechanisms and the accompanying changes in mechanical properties. This allows the construction of more reliable schemes or models of the microstructural degradation of heat-resistant materials, useful for engineering diagnostics. In austenitic steels, microstructural degradation is typically described as a sequence of precipitation processes. This requires microscopic examination in the laboratory to identify secondary-phase precipitates.

The operational safety and stability of power units depend on their correct diagnostics, which in turn depend, among other things, on the availability of reliable material characteristics. The material data, based on laboratory tests that form the basis of these characteristics, are less prone to error when results are obtained from long-term experiments. The paper presents the results of research on the degradation of the S31035 alloy microstructure after long-term ageing at 750 °C, with emphasis on precipitation processes at grain boundaries and within grains.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs: The research was conducted on S31035 (22Cr25Ni3W3CuCoNbN) steel, with the chemical composition presented in Table  1 . Test specimens were taken from a pipe section of 38.0 × 8.8 mm. The ageing process was carried out at 750 °C for up to 30,000 h.
The microstructure of the test steel was observed using a ZEISS SUPRA 35 scanning electron microscope (SEM) on conventionally prepared electrolytically etched metallographic sections.

The identification of precipitates in the test steel was carried out using a FEI S/TEM TITAN 80–300 high-resolution electron microscope. The microscope was additionally equipped with a Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (STEM) scanning system, as well as Bright Field (BF), Dark Field (DF), and High-Angle Annular Dark Field (HAADF) scanning and transmission detectors. It also featured a Cs condenser spherical aberration corrector and an energy-dispersion spectrometer (EDS). Precipitate phase identification was performed on thin foils using the selective electron diffraction method. In addition, the precipitates were observed using Scanning Electron Microscopy - Backscattered Electrons (SEM-BSE).

sections.heading: Microstructure of the as-received condition
paragraphs: Heat-resistant austenitic stainless steels are delivered in the heat-treated state, specifically through solution heat treatment. Consequently, their microstructure in this state is an austenite matrix, characterised by numerous annealing twins and primary precipitations (Fig.  1 ). These precipitates were identified as the Z phase (Fig.  2 ), i.e. a complex nitride (CrNbN), rich in both niobium and chromium (Figs.  2 ,  3 ). The tested steel contains carbide-forming elements in its chemical composition (Cr, W, Nb)—Table  1 , but niobium is a very strong carbide–forming element mentioned above; hence, in the as-received state, numerous Z-phase precipitates rich in this element are visible in the microstructure (Figs.  1 ,  2 ). The EDS microanalysis of these phases demonstrates that the Z phase is enriched by niobium by about 80 wt%—Fig.  2 .
Fig. 1 Microstructure of as-received S31035 steel, SEM
Fig. 2 Primary Z phase precipitation( a ) with resolved diffraction ( b ) and EDS spectrum ( c )

Primary precipitates in austenitic steels are formed in the last stage of crystallisation [ 14 ]. This results in the presence of these precipitates at grain boundaries and within grains. The primary precipitates are characterised by high thermal stability [ 15 ]; however, due to their micrometric dimensions, they do not significantly affect the strengthening of the tested alloy. Their function is limited to partially binding carbon and/or nitrogen atoms, and limiting grain growth during thermoplastic treatment. In the as-received condition, i.e., after solution heat treatment, the dominant hardening mechanism in austenitic steels is solution hardening; hence, these alloys are characterised in the initial condition by relatively low strength and good/very good plastic properties and ductility (toughness).

The metastable microstructure of supersaturated austenitic steel will gradually evolve during long-term service/ageing. Precipitation processes and changes in the morphology of secondary phase precipitates in austenitic steels are the basic mechanism in the degradation of the microstructure and mechanical properties of these alloys. Precipitation processes in these alloys are observed at grain boundaries and inside grains.

sections.heading: Precipitation processes at the boundaries: steel after ageing
paragraphs: We know that grain boundaries in the alloy are preferred sites for particle precipitation. Grain boundaries as surface defects are characterised by high surface energy compared to the grain interiors or twin boundaries. Also, atomic diffusion is significantly faster compared to the inside of the grain. The type of grain boundaries significantly influences the precipitate process in austenitic stainless steel. In austenitic steels, the preferred grain boundaries for the initial precipitation of secondary phase particles are boundaries with high misorientation and a high degree of coincidence [ 16 ].
In the initial stage of ageing, chromium—rich M 23 C 6  carbides were revealed on the grain boundaries of the alloy austenite (Figs.  3 ,  4 ).
Fig. 3 The M 23 C 6  precipitate after ageing in the S31035 steel, TEM
Fig. 4 Distribution map of alloying elements in S31035 steel after ageing and EDS spectrum of M 23 C 6  carbide and matrix

The preferential and relatively rapid precipitation of Cr-rich M 23 C 6  carbides (Fig.  4 ) at grain boundaries is mainly related to the supersaturation of the matrix with vacancies, chromium atoms and limited solubility of carbon. Initially, fine M 23 C 6  carbides precipitated at the grain boundaries contributed to the hindering of dislocation slip along the boundaries and inhibited boundary migration, which prevents the matrix softening processes [ 17 ]. The effective inhibition of dislocation movement by these precipitates contributes to increased precipitation strengthening, resulting in enhanced strength properties and improved creep resistance. At the same time, the appearance of secondary phase particles at grain boundaries contributes to a significant reduction in the ductility and plasticity of austenitic alloys. The M 23 C 6  carbides precipitated at grain boundaries in coarse-grained HR3C steel contribute to the decrease in fracture energy by about 80–90% after several hundred hours of ageing [ 18 ].

The M 23 C 6  carbides are characterised by low thermodynamic stability [ 18 ], which is related to their high interphase boundary energy and translates into an increase in their size with ageing (Fig.  5 a) and the formation of the so-called continuous grid of precipitates at the boundaries (Fig.  6 ).
Fig. 5 The average diameter of M 23 C 6  ( a ), Laves phase ( b ), sigma phase ( c ) precipitates in S31035 as a function of ageing time

The initial increase in the size of M 23 C 6  carbides at the grain boundaries (Fig.  5 a) is related to short-range diffusion [ 18 ]. The diffusion of chromium atoms from the boundary areas to the M 23 C 6  carbides precipitating and growing at the grain boundaries contributes to the sensitization of steel, resulting in the formation of Cr-depleted zones. The steel becomes susceptible to intergranular corrosion [ 19 ]. Still, at longer heating times, particle growth must be supported by long-range chromium atom diffusion. The presence of tungsten and boron microaddition in the chemical composition of the tested steel (Table  1 ) suggests the possibility of enrichment of M 23 C 6  carbides with atoms of these elements (Fig.  4 ).
Fig. 6 Continuous grid of precipitates in the microstructure of S31035 steel, SEM

The presence of tungsten and boron in M 23 C 6  carbides increases the stability of these precipitates as a result of the reduction of the particle/matrix interfacial energy [ 20 ]. The beneficial effect of the addition of these elements on reducing the tendency of M 23 C 6  carbides to kaolinization was observed in martensitic steels of the 9–12%Cr type [ 21 ]. However, in the tested steel, an increase in the size of M 23 C 6  carbides was visible (Fig.  5 a), indicating that the beneficial effect of these elements was time-limited.

In addition to M 23 C 6  carbides, Laves phase precipitates were also revealed at the grain boundaries (Fig.  7 a). The Laves phase precipitates were rich in tungsten (Fig.  8 ). The nucleation and growth of the Laves phase particles take place independently [ 22 ]. These precipitates are mainly observed at the M 23 C 6  carbide/matrix interface boundary. In the case of nucleation and growth at the interphase boundary, this is due to the limited solubility of tungsten in these carbides, which results in enrichment at the interphase boundary. The presence of silicon in the Lavesphase precipitates at the grain boundaries (Fig.  8 ) confirms its important role as a Laves phase promotion element. The enrichment of the Laves phase results from the limited solubility of silicon in M 23 C 6  carbides, as well as in the austenitic matrix (silicon is a ferrite-forming element). Resulting in enrichment of micro-areas with this element, stimulating the precipitation of the Laves phase. The effect of this is preferential precipitation of the Laves phase at grain boundaries near carbides M 23 C 6  (Fig.  7 ). The important role of silicon in inducing the precipitation of the Laves phase in the microstructure of high chromium martensitic steels was also demonstrated in the work [ 23 ].
Fig. 7 The Laves phase after ageing in the S31035 steel, SEM
Fig. 8 Surface distribution of the main elements in the microstructure of S31035 steel after 30,000 h of ageing

The Laves phase particles, in contrast to M 23 C 6  carbides, show relatively high stability (Fig.  5 b), which is related to their half-coherent interphase boundary. The limitation of the growth rate of Laves phase precipitates is related not only to the low value of the interfacial energy, but also to the fact that the Laves phase is a tungsten-rich precipitate (Fig.  8 ). Tungsten in the Laves phase, similarly to M 23 C 6  carbides, reduces the interfacial energy value [ 20 ], which helps to limit the coagulation rate (Fig.  5 b). However, as in the case of M 23 C 6  carbides, an increase in the size of this phase is observed after incubation time. Due to the limited growth rate of this phase, some researchers [ 22 ] indicate that the Laves phase precipitation should be treated as a form of grain boundary precipitation strengthening. The Laves phase’s effect on the properties of a given alloy depends on its volume fraction. A larger surface share of the Laves phase precipitated at the boundaries increases creep resistance by inhibiting dislocation slip at the boundaries, similar to M 23 C 6  carbides. The Laves phase precipitates negatively affect ductility and elongation determined in the creep test and reduce high-temperature strength properties determined in the static tensile test [ 22 ]. A detailed description of the kinetics of precipitation and growth of Laves phase precipitates in the tested steel is presented in [ 11 ].

When the chromium equivalent value, Cr eq , calculated from Eq. ( 1 ), is above 17–18% by weight, the steel has a strong tendency to precipitate the sigma phase. For the tested steel, the Cr eq  value is 21.90%. The tested steel shows a high tendency to precipitate the sigma phase during operation.
Fig. 9 The sigma phase after ageing in the S31035 steel, SEM
Fig. 10 Distribution map of alloying elements in S31035 steel after ageing and EDS spectrum of sigma phase
Fig. 11 The sigma phase precipitation ( a ) with resolved diffraction ( b ) and EDS spectrum ( c ) after ageing in the S31035 steel, TEM

The rate of sigma phase precipitation in the structure of austenitic steels depends mainly on the chromium content in the steel (see Eq. ( 1 )), but the above is also influenced by the content of titanium and niobium in the chemical composition of the alloy. Strong carbide-forming elements bind carbon or nitrogen atoms, thereby increasing the activity and amount of chromium in the matrix. The acceleration of this phase’s occurrence in the microstructure is also influenced by grain size and microstructural defects, such as strain–induced precipitation [ 25 ].

The sigma phase in austenitic stainless steel may precipitate due to the decomposition of delta ferrite, nucleating in situ on M 23 C 6  carbides and independently of the matrix [ 25 ]. In the tested steel, sigma phase precipitates were detected at the contact of three grain boundaries, near the M 23 C 6  carbides and Laves phase (Figs.  9 ,  10 ). The precipitation of the sigma phase near the chromium-rich M 23 C 6  carbides (Fig.  4 ) is related to the higher energy of nucleation activation at the interphase boundary compared to the grain interior and the fact that these carbides constitute the “source” of the chromium atoms necessary for the formation of the sigma phase. In turn, the precipitation of the sigma phase near the Laves phase precipitates results from the limited solubility of chromium in the Laves phase. Therefore, the precipitated Laves-phase particles enrich the interphase boundary with chromium, thereby promoting the possible nucleation and growth of the sigma phase. According to [ 26 ], the precipitation of the Laves phase in austenitic steels directly precedes the occurrence of sigma phase precipitates. The sigma phase, similarly to M 23 C 6  carbides, is characterised by low stability, which causes an increase in the particle size of this phase during ageing (Fig.  5 c). The rapid increase in the sigma phase size is related to its high interfacial energy [ 20 ] and leads to its growth at the expense of the disappearance of the M 23 C 6  carbides precipitated at the boundaries. The effect of this is, among others, a reduction in the size of M 23 C 6  carbides (Fig.  5 a) and the formation of a continuous mesh by the sigma phase at the grain boundaries, what was observed in austeniticsteel after long-term operation [ 27 ].

The sigma phase precipitates are harmful and have an adverse effect on the plasticity and toughness of the steel, especially for coarse-grain steels. However, as our own research has shown, in the case of modern heat-resistant austenitic steels [ 28 ], the negative effect of the sigma phase on the reduction of plasticity and ductility is limited. The sigma phase, a chromium-rich precipitate, negatively affects the corrosion resistance of austenitic steel, particularly pitting corrosion. Its effect on creep resistance, in turn, depends on precipitate dispersion.

In addition to the above-mentioned precipitates at the grain boundaries following ageing at 750 °C, the presence of G phase precipitates, which were rich in chromium, nickel and silicon, was revealed (Fig.  12 ).
Fig. 12 The G phase precipitation ( a ) with resolved diffraction ( b ) and EDS spectrum ( c ) after ageing in the S31035 steel, TEM

The precipitates of this phase were revealed at the boundaries near M 23 C 6  carbides, as the G phase and M 23 C 6  carbide have similar lattice constants [ 28 ]. The precipitation of the G phase, according to [ 25 ], is related to the in situ transformation of M 23 C 6  carbides as a result of enriching them in silicon and nickel atoms. In turn, according to [ 26 ], the G phase can also be released as a result of the transformation of NbC particles. The progress of the M 23 C 6  → G phase transformation depends on the rate of diffusion of silicon (and nickel) atoms. The limited solubility of silicon and nickel atoms in M 23 C 6  carbides contributes to an increase in the silicon concentration in micro-areas at the interphase boundary, which favours the nucleation and growth of phases rich in these elements. Similar to precipitates of other particles observed at grain boundaries, the G phase precipitates have a negative effect, mainly on the toughness and ductility of the alloy [ 29 ]. The precipitation and growth of G phase particles, a nickel-rich phase (Fig.  12 ), can be accompanied by a depletion of nickel (austenite – forming element) in the matrix. This causes the matrix to become depleted of this element, which translates into a decrease in austenite stability and the appearance of ferrite in the structure.

The precipitations of the sigma phase and G phase at the grain boundaries take place at the expense of M 23 C 6  carbides and cause a visible change in the size of M 23 C 6  precipitates in the tested steel (Fig.  5 a). This led to the complete disappearance of these particles, with the above phases precipitating instead, as observed in the T321H steel after approximately 200,000 h of operation [ 27 ].

sections.heading: Precipitation processes within the grains: steel after ageing
paragraphs: The chemical composition of S31035 steel includes a copper additive (Table  1 ), leading to the release of particles rich in this element during ageing. The precipitation of numerous, very fine, coherent copper particles (Fig.  13 ) in an austenitic matrix. Copper-rich nanometric precipitates are observed in the tested steel during the initial ageing period.

Fig. 13 Precipitation of ε_Cu in S31035 steel:  a  STEM-BF image,  c  STEM-HAADF image of a single precipitate of ε_Cu, analysis of chemical composition in area B ( c ) and area A ( d ),  e  profile changes in chemical composition along the marked line (i.e. from area A),  e  STEM-HAADF image

The rapid precipitation of copper-rich dispersion particles is attributed to the limited solubility of copper in the austenite matrix (approximately 1% wt. Cu), which creates a strong chemical driving force for ε_Cu precipitate formation. The ε_Cu particles are observed on dislocations and near alignment faults (Figs.  8 ,  14 ), which is consistent with a strong tendency for copper atoms to segregate to lattice defects within grains. The dispersive form and high density of around 10 12  m 3  of these particles in the matrix contribute to their significant influence on the increase in strength and creep properties through precipitation hardening [ 31 ]. Coherent or semi-coherent interphase boundaries also characterise the ε_Cu precipitates; therefore, the nucleation barrier of ε_Cu particles and interfacial energy are low [ 32 ]. Dispersive ε_Cu particles in heat-resistant austenitic steels may be responsible for from 17% to 27% of the increase in the yield strength of these alloys [ 33 ]. At the same time, ε_Cu precipitates show relatively high dimensional stability during long-term holding of the alloy at elevated temperature. Bai [ 32 ] reported that ε_Cu particle precipitates, 10–15 nm in diameter, were formed after 10 h at 650 °C and further ageing to 10,000 h resulted in a highly stable Cu-rich precipitate of 32 nm in diameter. A similar process of increasing the size of ε_Cu particles at the nanometric scale was observed in [ 28 ].
Fig. 14 Precipitation of ε_Cu particles on dislocations, TEM

Apart from ε_Cu particles, the dispersion of secondary Z phase precipitates was revealed within the grains (Figs.  15 ,  16 ). Secondary precipitates of the Z phase, similarly to the primary precipitates (Fig.  2 ), are particles rich mainly in chromium and niobium (Fig.  16 ). The Z phase particles are mainly precipitated on dislocations. The precipitation of Z phase in austenitic steels is due to the in situ transformation of MX particles or independently in the matrix [ 34 ]. Regardless of the mechanism of Z phase precipitation, it is related to the diffusion of chromium atoms. Diffusion of substitution elements in the austenite matrix progresses more slowly than in the ferrite matrix, resulting in the appearance of this type of precipitate after a few hundred or even a few thousand hours. In addition, the half-coherent interphaseboundary of these particles and the reduced diffusion of chromium atoms in the matrix are also reflected in the high stability of the particles of this phase.
Fig. 15 Secondary Z phase precipitation ( a ) with resolved diffraction ( b ) and EDS spectrum ( c ), TEM
Fig. 16 The STEM-BF image of S31035 substructure after ageing and EDS spectrum, TEM

The dispersive form of these particles and their relatively high stability make them, similarly to ε_Cu precipitates, play an essential role in strengthening austenitic steels through precipitation hardening. The pinning force of Z phase and ε_Cu particles is 10 and 27 times higher, respectively, compared to that of M 23 C 6  carbides [ 31 ].
The W-rich Laves phase precipitates (Figs.  8 ,  17 ) were observed not only at the grain boundaries (Fig.  7 a), but also within the grains (Fig.  7 b).
Fig. 17 The STEM-BF image substructure and distribution maps of alloying elements in S31035 steel after ageing, TEM

These precipitates had a specific needle-shape (Figs.  16 ,  17 ), which was determined by the compromise between the distortion energy and the total surface energy. Needle precipitates of the Laves phase are formed inside the grains near dislocations, which is related not only to the high tendency to segregate this element, but also to faster diffusion inside the grains compared to other substitution elements [ 26 ]. The increase in the strength of the tested alloy was determined by numerous relatively small precipitates, which depended not only on the dispersion or volume fraction of a given type of precipitate but also on their shape. The needle-shaped precipitates of the Laves phase generate Perierls–Nabarro stress about 46 MPa, while the precipitates with a shape close to spheroidal 28 MPa [ 11 ]. The precipitation hardening of S31035 steel resulting from dispersive Laves phase precipitates is comparable to the hardening resulting from the Z phase [ 34 ]. The correlation between a given state of the microstructure of austenitic matrix alloys—the degree of strengthening—and its mechanical properties is presented in the paper [ 35 ].

In addition to the above-mentioned secondary phase particles characterised by different morphologies in the microstructure of the test steel, single compound precipitate complexes were observed near grain boundaries (Fig.  18 ).
Fig. 18 The Z phase after ageing in the S31035 steel, TEM
Fig. 19 Complexes of precipitates in the S31035 steel, TEM

These complexes consisted of the primary Z phase precipitate (Fig.  18 ) and of the Laves phase particles and M 23 C 6  carbides nucleating on them (Fig.  19 ). The heterogeneous nucleation of secondary phase particles on the primary Z phase precipitate is probably linked to the beneficial crystallographic relationships between these precipitates and the higher energy of nucleation activation at the interphase boundary than that within the grain. Compound complexes of precipitates are also observed in other heat-resistant alloys after ageing/service, e.g. CrMoV steels—“H-carbides” [ 36 ] and the HR6W nickel-based alloy [ 37 ]. The presence of precipitation complexes in the microstructure results from the tendency of the matrix to reduce its internal energy and from the fact of easier nucleation on the interphase boundary than in the matrix.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: The precipitation processes in the S31035 steel after long-term ageing of up to 30,000 h at 750 °C were analysed. In the as-received state, primary Z phase precipitates were observed in the supersaturated matrix of the tested alloy. The ageing process results in the precipitation of secondary phases at grain boundaries, twin boundaries, and within grains. At the grain boundaries, M 23 C 6  carbides and the Laves phase precipitates are observed during the initial period of ageing. Longer ageing times lead to the precipitation of the sigma phase, while the G phase is observed after the longest holding time at the ageing temperature. At the twin boundaries, only M 23 C 6  carbides were observed. On the other hand, within the grains, the dispersive, ε_Cu and Z phase particles, and the Laves phase precipitates are observed. In addition, single complexes of precipitates consisting of the primary Z phase particles and M 23 C 6  carbides nucleating on them as well as the Laves phase precipitates were revealed near the grain boundaries in the microstructure of the test steel.
